organisms.morphology: Trophozoite (10-60 μm, motile, erythrophagocytosis) and cyst (10-20 μm, up to 4 nuclei)
organisms.transmission: Fecal-oral, ingestion of mature cysts in contaminated food/water
organisms.lifecycle: Cyst ingested → excystation in small intestine → trophozoites colonize colon → encystation → cysts passed in stool
organisms.diagnosis: Stool microscopy (cysts/trophozoites), antigen detection ELISA, PCR to distinguish from E. dispar
organisms.treatment: Metronidazole (invasive disease) + luminal agent (paromomycin) to eliminate cysts
organisms.geographicDistribution: Worldwide, especially tropics with poor sanitation

organisms.morphology: Non-pathogenic commensal; cyst has up to 8 nuclei
organisms.transmission: Fecal-oral
organisms.lifecycle: Same as E. histolytica but non-invasive
organisms.diagnosis: Stool microscopy, must be distinguished from E. histolytica
organisms.treatment: None required
organisms.geographicDistribution: Worldwide

organisms.morphology: Pear-shaped trophozoite with 2 nuclei and 4 pairs of flagella ('face' appearance); oval cyst with 4 nuclei
organisms.transmission: Fecal-oral, waterborne (resistant to chlorination)
organisms.lifecycle: Cyst ingested → excystation in duodenum → trophozoites attach to mucosa via ventral disc → encystation → cysts shed
organisms.diagnosis: Stool microscopy (cysts/trophozoites), antigen detection, string test/duodenal aspirate
organisms.treatment: Metronidazole or tinidazole
organisms.geographicDistribution: Worldwide, common in travelers and daycare settings

organisms.morphology: Pear-shaped, motile trophozoite only (no cyst stage), 4 anterior flagella + undulating membrane
organisms.transmission: Sexual transmission
organisms.lifecycle: Direct transmission between hosts, no environmental cyst stage
organisms.diagnosis: Wet mount microscopy of vaginal/urethral secretions, NAAT
organisms.treatment: Metronidazole or tinidazole (treat both partners)
organisms.geographicDistribution: Worldwide

organisms.morphology: Largest human protozoan parasite; ciliated trophozoite, macro/micronucleus; encysted form
organisms.transmission: Fecal-oral, especially from pigs (zoonotic)
organisms.lifecycle: Cyst ingested → excystation in colon → trophozoites can invade mucosa
clinicalManifestations: Diarrhea, dysentery, colonic ulceration (rare, usually mild/asymptomatic)
organisms.diagnosis: Stool microscopy — large ciliated trophozoites/cysts
organisms.treatment: Tetracycline or metronidazole
organisms.geographicDistribution: Worldwide, associated with pig farming

organisms.morphology: Oocysts 4-6 μm, intracellular but extracytoplasmic location in intestinal epithelium
organisms.transmission: Fecal-oral, waterborne (highly chlorine-resistant), zoonotic
organisms.lifecycle: Oocyst ingested → sporozoites invade enterocytes → asexual/sexual cycles → oocysts shed (auto-infective)
organisms.diagnosis: Modified Ziehl-Neelsen stain of stool, antigen ELISA, PCR
organisms.treatment: Nitazoxanide (immunocompetent); ART reconstitution in HIV patients
organisms.geographicDistribution: Worldwide, major cause of waterborne outbreaks

organisms.morphology: Large ellipsoidal oocysts (20-30 μm) with 2 sporoblasts
organisms.transmission: Fecal-oral
organisms.lifecycle: Similar coccidian cycle, intracellular in enterocytes
clinicalManifestations: Chronic watery diarrhea, especially in AIDS patients
organisms.diagnosis: Modified Ziehl-Neelsen stain, autofluorescence under UV microscopy
organisms.treatment: Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX)
organisms.geographicDistribution: Tropics/subtropics, HIV-associated worldwide

organisms.morphology: Oocysts 8-10 μm, autofluorescent under UV light
organisms.transmission: Fecal-oral, contaminated fresh produce/water
organisms.lifecycle: Requires environmental sporulation before becoming infectious (unlike Cryptosporidium)
clinicalManifestations: Prolonged watery diarrhea, fatigue, weight loss; relapsing pattern
organisms.diagnosis: Modified Ziehl-Neelsen (variable acid-fastness), UV autofluorescence, PCR
organisms.treatment: TMP-SMX
organisms.geographicDistribution: Worldwide, linked to imported fresh produce outbreaks

organisms.morphology: Sporocysts in stool (intestinal form) or sarcocysts in muscle (muscular form)
organisms.transmission: Ingestion of undercooked meat containing sarcocysts
organisms.lifecycle: Two-host cycle: herbivore (intermediate) → carnivore/human (definitive, intestinal form)
clinicalManifestations: Usually asymptomatic; mild GI symptoms or myositis (muscular form)
organisms.diagnosis: Stool microscopy for sporocysts, muscle biopsy for sarcocysts
organisms.treatment: Usually self-limited; no established standard therapy
organisms.geographicDistribution: Worldwide, higher in areas eating raw/undercooked meat

organisms.morphology: Highly pleomorphic — vacuolar, granular, amoeboid, cyst forms
organisms.transmission: Fecal-oral
organisms.lifecycle: Not fully elucidated; cyst form considered infective stage
clinicalManifestations: Possible association with IBS-like symptoms in some patients
organisms.diagnosis: Stool microscopy, PCR
organisms.treatment: Treatment controversial; metronidazole if symptomatic and no other cause found
organisms.geographicDistribution: Worldwide, very common finding in stool exams

organisms.morphology: Elongated trypomastigote with undulating membrane and free flagellum in blood/CSF
organisms.transmission: Tsetse fly bite (Glossina spp.)
organisms.lifecycle: Fly injects metacyclic trypomastigotes → bloodstream/lymphatics → CNS invasion (late stage)
clinicalManifestations: African sleeping sickness: chancre, fever, lymphadenopathy (Winterbottom's sign)
Late stage: meningoencephalitis, sleep-wake cycle disruption, coma
organisms.diagnosis: Blood/lymph node aspirate/CSF microscopy, CATT serology (gambiense)
organisms.treatment: Pentamidine/suramin (hemolymphatic stage); melarsoprol/eflornithine (CNS stage)
organisms.geographicDistribution: Sub-Saharan Africa (gambiense: West/Central; rhodesiense: East Africa)

organisms.morphology: Trypomastigote (blood, C-shaped) and amastigote (intracellular, tissue)
organisms.transmission: Triatomine ('kissing bug') feces contaminating bite wound; also congenital, transfusion, oral (contaminated food)
organisms.lifecycle: Bug feces contain metacyclic trypomastigotes → enter through bite site/mucosa → intracellular amastigote replication → trypomastigotes released into blood
clinicalManifestations: Acute: Romaña's sign (periorbital edema), chagoma, fever
Chronic: cardiomyopathy, megaesophagus, megacolon (10-30 years later)
organisms.diagnosis: Acute: blood smear/PCR. Chronic: serology (2 different tests)
organisms.treatment: Benznidazole or nifurtimox (most effective in acute phase)
organisms.geographicDistribution: Latin America (Chagas disease)

organisms.morphology: Amastigote (intracellular, in macrophages) and promastigote (flagellated, in sandfly)
organisms.transmission: Sandfly bite (Phlebotomus/Lutzomyia)
organisms.lifecycle: Sandfly injects promastigotes → phagocytosed by macrophages → transform to amastigotes → replicate → new sandfly ingests amastigotes → transform back to promastigotes
clinicalManifestations: Visceral leishmaniasis (kala-azar): fever, hepatosplenomegaly, pancytopenia — fatal if untreated
organisms.diagnosis: Tissue/bone marrow/splenic aspirate microscopy (amastigotes), culture (NNN medium), serology, PCR
organisms.treatment: Liposomal amphotericin B, pentavalent antimonials, miltefosine
organisms.geographicDistribution: Tropics/subtropics, Mediterranean basin, Latin America, South Asia, East Africa

organisms.morphology: Tachyzoite (acute, crescent-shaped), bradyzoite (tissue cyst, chronic), oocyst (cat feces)
organisms.transmission: Ingestion of oocysts (cat feces-contaminated food/water) or tissue cysts (undercooked meat); congenital (transplacental)
organisms.lifecycle: Definitive host: cats (sexual cycle, oocyst shedding). Intermediate hosts (humans, other mammals): tissue cyst formation after ingestion
clinicalManifestations: Immunocompetent: usually asymptomatic or mild mononucleosis-like illness
Congenital: chorioretinitis, hydrocephalus, intracranial calcifications (classic triad)
organisms.diagnosis: Serology (IgG/IgM, avidity testing for timing in pregnancy), PCR (amniotic fluid, CSF), imaging for cerebral lesions
organisms.treatment: Pyrimethamine + sulfadiazine + folinic acid; spiramycin in pregnancy (prevents transplacental transmission)
organisms.geographicDistribution: Worldwide

organisms.morphology: Adult tapeworm 4-10m, scolex with 4 suckers (no hooks), proglottids with 15-30 uterine branches
organisms.transmission: Ingestion of undercooked beef containing cysticerci
organisms.lifecycle: Human (definitive host) ingests larval cysticercus in beef → attaches to intestine → matures → gravid proglottids passed in stool → eggs ingested by cattle (intermediate host) → cysticerci form in muscle
clinicalManifestations: Passage of motile proglottids in stool/undergarments
organisms.diagnosis: Stool microscopy for eggs/proglottids, proglottid uterine branch counting for species ID
organisms.treatment: Praziquantel or niclosamide
organisms.geographicDistribution: Worldwide, beef-consuming regions

organisms.morphology: Adult tapeworm 2-7m, scolex with 4 suckers AND a rostellum with hooks, fewer uterine branches (7-13) than T. saginata
organisms.transmission: Adult worm: undercooked pork with cysticerci. Cysticercosis: fecal-oral ingestion of T. solium eggs
organisms.lifecycle: Same as T. saginata but pig is intermediate host; humans can also become accidental intermediate host (cysticercosis) if eggs are ingested
clinicalManifestations: Cysticercosis: subcutaneous nodules, neurocysticercosis (seizures, most common cause of adult-onset epilepsy in endemic areas)
organisms.diagnosis: Stool microscopy for taeniasis; imaging (CT/MRI) + serology for neurocysticercosis
organisms.treatment: Praziquantel/niclosamide (intestinal); albendazole + corticosteroids (neurocysticercosis, careful monitoring for inflammation)
organisms.geographicDistribution: Latin America, Asia, Sub-Saharan Africa (pork-consuming regions with poor sanitation)

organisms.morphology: Smallest human tapeworm (2-4 cm), only one requiring no intermediate host (can auto-infect)
organisms.transmission: Fecal-oral (direct, egg ingestion); can also involve insect intermediate hosts (fleas, beetles)
organisms.lifecycle: Egg ingested → larva develops in intestinal villus → matures to adult in lumen → autoinfection possible (unique among tapeworms)
clinicalManifestations: Heavy infection: abdominal pain, diarrhea, irritability in children
organisms.diagnosis: Stool microscopy for characteristic eggs (polar filaments)
organisms.treatment: Praziquantel
organisms.geographicDistribution: Worldwide, especially in children in crowded/poor-hygiene settings

organisms.morphology: Longest human tapeworm (up to 10m+), scolex with 2 sucking grooves (bothria), thousands of proglottids
organisms.transmission: Ingestion of undercooked/raw freshwater fish containing plerocercoid larvae
organisms.lifecycle: Eggs in water → coracidium → ingested by copepod → procercoid → fish ingests copepod → plerocercoid in fish muscle → human eats fish
clinicalManifestations: Vitamin B12 deficiency/megaloblastic anemia (worm competes for B12)
organisms.diagnosis: Stool microscopy for operculated eggs
organisms.treatment: Praziquantel
organisms.geographicDistribution: Cold freshwater lake regions (Scandinavia, Baltic, Great Lakes, Japan)

organisms.morphology: Small tapeworm, proglottids resemble cucumber/rice seeds, double set of genital organs per proglottid
organisms.transmission: Accidental ingestion of infected fleas (mainly affects dogs/cats; rare in humans, mostly children)
organisms.lifecycle: Flea larva ingests tapeworm eggs → develops cysticercoid → dog/cat/human ingests infected flea → adult develops in intestine
clinicalManifestations: Mild GI upset, passage of proglottids
organisms.diagnosis: Stool microscopy for characteristic egg packets or proglottids
organisms.treatment: Praziquantel
organisms.geographicDistribution: Worldwide, wherever dogs/cats and fleas coexist with humans

organisms.morphology: Adult (in dog) tiny 3-6mm; larval hydatid cyst in human — fluid-filled, unilocular, with germinal layer producing protoscolices
organisms.transmission: Fecal-oral ingestion of eggs from dog feces (dogs = definitive host, sheep/humans = intermediate/accidental host)
organisms.lifecycle: Dog sheds eggs → sheep (or human) ingests eggs → oncosphere migrates to liver/lung → develops into hydatid cyst → dog eats infected offal → adult worm develops in dog intestine
clinicalManifestations: Cystic echinococcosis (hydatid disease): slow-growing cysts in liver (65%) or lung (25%)
organisms.diagnosis: Imaging (ultrasound/CT showing cyst with daughter cysts), serology (indirect hemagglutination, ELISA)
organisms.treatment: Surgical removal (PAIR technique: puncture-aspiration-injection-reaspiration) + albendazole
organisms.geographicDistribution: Sheep-raising regions: Mediterranean, Middle East, South America, Central Asia

organisms.morphology: Fluid-filled cysticercus with invaginated scolex, found in muscle, subcutaneous tissue, brain, eye
organisms.transmission: Ingestion of T. solium eggs (fecal-oral, autoinfection possible)
organisms.lifecycle: Egg ingested → oncosphere penetrates gut wall → hematogenous spread → cysticercus forms in tissues
organisms.diagnosis: CT/MRI (calcified or cystic lesions), serology (EITB)
organisms.treatment: Albendazole/praziquantel + corticosteroids (active neurocysticercosis); surgery for ocular/ventricular disease
organisms.geographicDistribution: Latin America, Sub-Saharan Africa, Asia

organisms.morphology: Coenurus: larger cyst than cysticercus, contains multiple protoscolices (invaginated scolices) budding from germinal membrane
organisms.transmission: Fecal-oral ingestion of Taenia multiceps eggs from dog feces (dogs = definitive host, sheep/humans = intermediate)
organisms.lifecycle: Egg ingested → oncosphere migrates → coenurus develops (mainly CNS, subcutaneous tissue)
clinicalManifestations: Cerebral coenurosis: increased intracranial pressure, seizures
organisms.diagnosis: Imaging (CT/MRI), histopathology after excision
organisms.treatment: Surgical excision (definitive), albendazole as adjunct
organisms.geographicDistribution: Sheep-raising regions of Africa

organisms.morphology: Sparganum: ribbon-like migrating larva (plerocercoid of Spirometra spp.)
organisms.transmission: Ingestion of infected copepods (drinking water), undercooked frog/snake meat, or traditional poultice application of infected flesh to wounds/eyes
organisms.lifecycle: Copepod → frog/snake/bird (paratenic hosts) → definitive host (cat/dog) OR accidental human infection via ingestion/skin contact
clinicalManifestations: Ocular sparganosis (periorbital swelling, can cause blindness if untreated)
organisms.diagnosis: Surgical excision + histopathology, serology where available
organisms.treatment: Surgical removal of larva (definitive); praziquantel of uncertain efficacy
organisms.geographicDistribution: East/Southeast Asia (traditional poultice practices increase risk)

organisms.morphology: Adult worms in copula (male grooves around female), eggs large lateral spine
organisms.transmission: Skin penetration by cercariae released from freshwater snails (Biomphalaria)
organisms.lifecycle: Egg in feces → miracidium hatches in water → infects snail → cercariae released → penetrate human skin → migrate to portal/mesenteric veins → adults produce eggs
clinicalManifestations: Chronic: intestinal/hepatosplenic disease, periportal (Symmers) fibrosis, portal hypertension
organisms.diagnosis: Stool microscopy for lateral-spined eggs, serology, rectal biopsy
organisms.treatment: Praziquantel
organisms.geographicDistribution: Sub-Saharan Africa, South America (Brazil), Caribbean, Middle East

organisms.morphology: Eggs with terminal spine, adults reside in vesical/pelvic venous plexus
organisms.transmission: Skin penetration by cercariae from Bulinus snails in freshwater
organisms.lifecycle: Same general schistosome cycle but adults migrate to bladder venous plexus
clinicalManifestations: Increased risk of squamous cell bladder carcinoma
organisms.diagnosis: Urine microscopy for terminal-spined eggs (collect midday), cystoscopy
organisms.treatment: Praziquantel
organisms.geographicDistribution: Africa, Middle East

organisms.morphology: Eggs round with small lateral knob (rudimentary spine), produces most eggs per day of all schistosomes
organisms.transmission: Skin penetration by cercariae from Oncomelania snails
organisms.lifecycle: Same schistosome cycle, adults in mesenteric veins; zoonotic reservoir (cattle, dogs, pigs) important
clinicalManifestations: Most severe intestinal/hepatosplenic disease of the schistosomes due to high egg output
organisms.diagnosis: Stool microscopy, serology
organisms.treatment: Praziquantel
organisms.geographicDistribution: China, Philippines, Indonesia

organisms.morphology: Large leaf-shaped fluke (2-3cm), operculated eggs
organisms.transmission: Ingestion of metacercariae on aquatic vegetation (watercress) or contaminated water
organisms.lifecycle: Egg → miracidium → snail (Lymnaea) → cercariae → encyst as metacercariae on vegetation → ingested → migrate through gut wall/liver parenchyma → bile ducts
clinicalManifestations: Acute (hepatic migration): fever, RUQ pain, hepatomegaly, marked eosinophilia
organisms.diagnosis: Stool microscopy (eggs, may be delayed/negative in acute phase), serology (more useful acutely), imaging
organisms.treatment: Triclabendazole (drug of choice, praziquantel NOT effective)
organisms.geographicDistribution: Worldwide, sheep/cattle-raising areas (Andes, Europe, Middle East)

organisms.morphology: Small flukes (7-12mm) in bile ducts, operculated eggs with shoulder
organisms.transmission: Ingestion of undercooked/raw freshwater fish containing metacercariae
organisms.lifecycle: Egg → snail → cercariae → fish (metacercariae in muscle) → human ingestion → adults migrate to bile ducts
clinicalManifestations: Chronic infection strongly associated with cholangiocarcinoma
organisms.diagnosis: Stool microscopy for eggs, imaging
organisms.treatment: Praziquantel
organisms.geographicDistribution: Southeast Asia (Opisthorchis viverrini), Eastern Europe/Russia (O. felineus)

organisms.morphology: Thick, reddish-brown fluke, thick-shelled operculated eggs
organisms.transmission: Ingestion of undercooked freshwater crab/crayfish containing metacercariae
organisms.lifecycle: Egg → snail → cercariae → crab/crayfish (metacercariae) → ingested → migrate through diaphragm to lungs → adult pairs in cystic cavities
clinicalManifestations: Chronic cough with rusty/blood-tinged sputum (mimics TB)
organisms.diagnosis: Sputum/stool microscopy for eggs, imaging (nodular/cystic lung lesions), serology
organisms.treatment: Praziquantel or triclabendazole
organisms.geographicDistribution: East/Southeast Asia, West Africa, parts of Latin America

organisms.morphology: Small white worm (1cm), female migrates to perianal region at night to lay eggs, flattened eggs
organisms.transmission: Fecal-oral, autoinfection, fomites (highly contagious), retro-infection
organisms.lifecycle: Eggs ingested/inhaled → hatch in duodenum → mature in colon → gravid female migrates to perianal skin at night to deposit eggs → eggs become infective within hours
organisms.diagnosis: Scotch tape test (cellophane tape applied to perianal skin in morning)
organisms.treatment: Albendazole or mebendazole (treat whole household, repeat dose in 2 weeks)
organisms.geographicDistribution: Worldwide, most common helminth infection in developed countries

organisms.morphology: Whip-shaped worm, barrel-shaped eggs with bipolar plugs
organisms.transmission: Fecal-oral, ingestion of embryonated eggs from soil (geohelminth)
organisms.lifecycle: Eggs embryonate in soil (2-4 weeks) → ingested → larvae hatch in small intestine → migrate to cecum/colon → whipping anterior end embeds in mucosa
clinicalManifestations: Heavy infection: bloody diarrhea, rectal prolapse (children), Trichuris dysentery syndrome
organisms.diagnosis: Stool microscopy for bipolar-plugged eggs
organisms.treatment: Albendazole or mebendazole
organisms.geographicDistribution: Tropics/subtropics with poor sanitation

organisms.morphology: Largest intestinal nematode (up to 35cm female), thick mammillated (bumpy) shell eggs
organisms.transmission: Fecal-oral, ingestion of embryonated eggs from contaminated soil/food (geohelminth)
organisms.lifecycle: Eggs embryonate in soil → ingested → larvae hatch, penetrate gut wall → migrate via bloodstream to lungs (Löffler pneumonia) → coughed up, swallowed → mature to adult in small intestine
clinicalManifestations: Löffler syndrome (pulmonary phase): cough, wheezing, eosinophilia
Heavy infection: intestinal obstruction, biliary/pancreatic duct obstruction
organisms.diagnosis: Stool microscopy for mammillated eggs, imaging for obstruction, worm visible on imaging/passed in stool
organisms.treatment: Albendazole or mebendazole
organisms.geographicDistribution: Worldwide, especially tropics with poor sanitation — most common human helminth infection

organisms.morphology: Adult worms tiny in intestine; larvae encyst in striated muscle (coiled, 'nurse cell')
organisms.transmission: Ingestion of undercooked meat (pork, wild boar, bear) containing encysted larvae
organisms.lifecycle: Larvae released in stomach → mature to adults in intestine → produce new larvae → migrate via bloodstream to striated muscle → encyst
clinicalManifestations: Muscular invasion phase: myalgia, periorbital edema, fever, marked eosinophilia
organisms.diagnosis: Serology, muscle biopsy, marked eosinophilia + elevated CK
organisms.treatment: Albendazole/mebendazole + corticosteroids for severe symptoms
organisms.geographicDistribution: Worldwide, wherever undercooked pork/game meat is consumed

organisms.morphology: Adult female extremely long (up to 1m), emerges through skin blister
organisms.transmission: Ingestion of copepods (Cyclops) containing infective larvae in drinking water
organisms.lifecycle: Copepod ingested → larvae released → penetrate gut wall → mature, mate → gravid female migrates to subcutaneous tissue (usually lower limb) → forms blister → releases larvae into water on contact
organisms.diagnosis: Clinical (visible worm), no lab test typically needed
organisms.treatment: Slow manual extraction (wrapping worm around stick over days-weeks), wound care; no effective drug
organisms.geographicDistribution: Near-eradicated; remaining foci in Chad, South Sudan, Ethiopia, Mali

organisms.morphology: Hookworm with cutting plates in buccal capsule, thin-shelled oval eggs
organisms.transmission: Skin penetration by filariform larvae from contaminated soil (also can be oral)
organisms.lifecycle: Eggs in soil → rhabditiform → filariform (infective) larvae → penetrate skin → bloodstream → lungs → coughed up, swallowed → attach to small intestine mucosa, blood-feeding
clinicalManifestations: Iron-deficiency anemia, protein loss (chronic blood loss from attachment sites)
organisms.diagnosis: Stool microscopy for eggs, occult blood in stool, anemia workup
organisms.treatment: Albendazole or mebendazole + iron supplementation
organisms.geographicDistribution: Worldwide tropics/subtropics, historically Southern Europe/Mediterranean

organisms.morphology: Hookworm with cutting plates (not teeth like Ancylostoma), similar eggs
organisms.transmission: Skin penetration by filariform larvae (strictly percutaneous, unlike A. duodenale)
organisms.lifecycle: Same as A. duodenale
clinicalManifestations: Same as A. duodenale but generally lower blood loss per worm
organisms.diagnosis: Stool microscopy (eggs indistinguishable from A. duodenale, larval culture needed to differentiate species)
organisms.treatment: Albendazole or mebendazole + iron supplementation
organisms.geographicDistribution: Americas, Sub-Saharan Africa, Asia, Pacific — most common hookworm worldwide

organisms.morphology: Only helminth capable of completing entire lifecycle within human host (autoinfection); larvae, not eggs, typically found in stool
organisms.transmission: Skin penetration by filariform larvae from soil; autoinfection cycle
organisms.lifecycle: Filariform larvae penetrate skin → lungs → trachea → swallowed → mature in intestine → can autoinfect (larvae reinfect host internally) — allows lifelong persistence
clinicalManifestations: Hyperinfection/disseminated strongyloidiasis in immunosuppressed (esp. corticosteroids, HTLV-1) — can be fatal, gram-negative sepsis from bowel translocation
organisms.diagnosis: Stool microscopy for larvae (multiple samples/agar plate culture for sensitivity), serology, screening before immunosuppression
organisms.treatment: Ivermectin (drug of choice)
organisms.geographicDistribution: Tropics/subtropics worldwide

organisms.morphology: Thread-like adult worms in lymphatics; sheathed microfilariae in blood with nocturnal periodicity
organisms.transmission: Culex, Anopheles, or Aedes mosquito bite
organisms.lifecycle: Mosquito injects L3 larvae → migrate to lymphatics → mature to adults → produce microfilariae → circulate in blood (nocturnal periodicity, matching vector biting time) → ingested by mosquito
organisms.diagnosis: Nocturnal blood smear (thick smear) for microfilariae, antigen detection (ICT card test), ultrasound (filarial dance sign)
organisms.treatment: Diethylcarbamazine (DEC) — avoid in areas co-endemic with onchocerciasis/loiasis; ivermectin + albendazole for mass drug administration
organisms.geographicDistribution: Sub-Saharan Africa, South Asia, Pacific Islands

organisms.morphology: Similar to W. bancrofti but smaller, sheathed microfilariae with characteristic nuclei pattern
organisms.transmission: Mansonia, Anopheles mosquito bite
organisms.lifecycle: Same general filarial cycle as W. bancrofti, nocturnal periodicity
clinicalManifestations: Lymphatic filariasis, typically affecting limbs below knee/elbow (more localized than W. bancrofti)
organisms.diagnosis: Nocturnal blood smear, PCR
organisms.treatment: Diethylcarbamazine (DEC)
organisms.geographicDistribution: South and Southeast Asia

organisms.morphology: Adult worm migrates visibly under skin/conjunctiva; unsheathed microfilariae with diurnal periodicity
organisms.transmission: Chrysops (deer/mango fly) bite
organisms.lifecycle: Fly injects L3 larvae → mature to adults migrating through subcutaneous tissue → microfilariae in blood with diurnal periodicity (matches fly's daytime biting)
clinicalManifestations: Eye worm — visible migration across conjunctiva
Risk of severe encephalopathy with ivermectin if high microfilarial load
organisms.diagnosis: Daytime blood smear for microfilariae, visual identification of adult worm in eye
organisms.treatment: Diethylcarbamazine (DEC); caution with ivermectin if co-infected/high loads due to encephalopathy risk
organisms.geographicDistribution: Central and West Africa rainforest belt

organisms.morphology: Adults in subcutaneous nodules; unsheathed microfilariae found in skin (not blood)
organisms.transmission: Simulium (black fly) bite near fast-flowing rivers
organisms.lifecycle: Black fly injects L3 larvae → mature into adults in subcutaneous nodules → microfilariae migrate through skin and eyes
organisms.diagnosis: Skin snip microscopy for microfilariae, slit-lamp exam (microfilariae in cornea/anterior chamber), nodule palpation/biopsy
organisms.treatment: Ivermectin (repeated dosing, kills microfilariae not adults); doxycycline (targets Wolbachia endosymbiont, weakens/sterilizes adults)
organisms.geographicDistribution: Sub-Saharan Africa (riverine areas), small foci in Yemen, Latin America

organisms.morphology: Small filariae; M. perstans/ozzardi unsheathed microfilariae in blood, M. streptocerca in skin
organisms.transmission: Culicoides (biting midge) bite
organisms.lifecycle: Midge injects L3 larvae → adults develop in body cavities/subcutaneous tissue → microfilariae in blood or skin depending on species
organisms.diagnosis: Blood smear (perstans/ozzardi) or skin snip (streptocerca) for microfilariae
organisms.treatment: Doxycycline (M. perstans, targets Wolbachia) or DEC/ivermectin depending on species
organisms.geographicDistribution: Sub-Saharan Africa (perstans/streptocerca), Central/South America Caribbean (ozzardi)

organisms.morphology: Covers key vector groups: mosquitoes (Anopheles, Culex, Aedes), flies (Glossina, Simulium, Phlebotomus, Chrysops, Culicoides), ticks, mites, lice, fleas, triatomine bugs
organisms.transmission: Vectors transmit pathogens via bite (inoculation), feces contamination, or mechanical carriage
organisms.lifecycle: Varies by vector; most arthropods of medical importance undergo egg-larva-pupa-adult (holometabolous) or egg-nymph-adult (hemimetabolous) development
clinicalManifestations: Direct effects: bites, allergic reactions, myiasis, scabies, pediculosis
organisms.diagnosis: Vector identification (morphology, geographic distribution), entomological surveillance
organisms.treatment: Vector control (insecticides, bed nets, environmental management), personal protection (repellents)
organisms.geographicDistribution: Varies by vector species

organisms.morphology: Budding yeast, pseudohyphae/true hyphae (C. albicans), germ tube positive (C. albicans specific test)
organisms.transmission: Endogenous (normal commensal flora overgrowth); rarely person-to-person (neonatal, sexual)
organisms.lifecycle: Commensal of skin/mucosa/GI tract; becomes pathogenic with disrupted flora, immunosuppression, or mucosal barrier breach
clinicalManifestations: Oral thrush, vulvovaginal candidiasis, cutaneous candidiasis (intertrigo, diaper rash)
organisms.diagnosis: Direct exam (KOH mount showing pseudohyphae), culture on Sabouraud agar, germ tube test, blood cultures for invasive disease
organisms.treatment: Topical/oral azoles (fluconazole) for mucocutaneous; echinocandins or amphotericin B for invasive disease
organisms.geographicDistribution: Worldwide

organisms.morphology: Round/oval yeast requiring lipid supplementation for culture ('spaghetti and meatballs' appearance on KOH with short hyphae)
organisms.transmission: Endogenous skin commensal, overgrowth-driven disease
organisms.lifecycle: Normal skin flora (sebaceous areas); disease occurs with heat, humidity, sebum changes, immunosuppression
clinicalManifestations: Pityriasis versicolor: hypo/hyperpigmented scaly patches on trunk
Seborrheic dermatitis: scaly erythematous plaques on scalp/face
organisms.diagnosis: KOH direct exam (short hyphae + spores), Wood's lamp (yellow-green fluorescence in versicolor), culture requires lipid-supplemented media
organisms.treatment: Topical antifungals (ketoconazole shampoo/cream, selenium sulfide); oral itraconazole for extensive disease
organisms.geographicDistribution: Worldwide, more common in hot/humid climates

organisms.morphology: Round yeast with thick polysaccharide capsule, visible by India ink preparation (halo effect)
organisms.transmission: Inhalation of desiccated yeast/spores from soil contaminated with bird droppings (neoformans) or eucalyptus trees (gattii)
organisms.lifecycle: Inhaled into lungs → primary pulmonary infection (often subclinical) → hematogenous dissemination, especially to CNS (neurotropism)
organisms.diagnosis: India ink stain of CSF, cryptococcal antigen (CrAg) test (blood/CSF, highly sensitive), culture on Sabouraud agar
organisms.treatment: Liposomal amphotericin B + flucytosine (induction) → fluconazole (consolidation/maintenance)
organisms.geographicDistribution: Worldwide (neoformans); gattii in tropical/subtropical regions (Australia, Pacific Northwest)

organisms.morphology: Very small spores (1-3 μm) with polar tubule for host cell invasion
organisms.transmission: Fecal-oral, ingestion/inhalation of spores, possibly zoonotic/waterborne
organisms.lifecycle: Spore injects sporoplasm into host cell via polar tubule → intracellular replication → new spores released upon cell rupture
clinicalManifestations: Chronic diarrhea in AIDS patients (E. bieneusi most common)
organisms.diagnosis: Modified trichrome stain (Weber-green) of stool, electron microscopy, PCR
organisms.treatment: Albendazole (Encephalitozoon); fumagillin or ART immune reconstitution (E. bieneusi, less responsive to albendazole)
organisms.geographicDistribution: Worldwide, mainly in immunocompromised patients

organisms.morphology: Cyst (5-8 μm, cup-shaped) and trophic forms; cannot be cultured routinely
organisms.transmission: Airborne person-to-person (respiratory droplets); most humans colonized/exposed in childhood
organisms.lifecycle: Extracellular in alveoli; disease occurs upon immunosuppression (CD4 <200 in HIV) allowing proliferation
clinicalManifestations: Pneumocystis pneumonia (PCP/PJP): insidious dyspnea, dry cough, fever in immunosuppressed
Diffuse bilateral interstitial infiltrates, elevated LDH
organisms.diagnosis: Bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) with methenamine silver stain or immunofluorescence, PCR
organisms.treatment: Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX) first line; prophylaxis in HIV with CD4 <200
organisms.geographicDistribution: Worldwide

organisms.morphology: Septate hyphae invading keratin (skin, hair, nails); macroconidia shape differs by genus (spindle: Microsporum, cigar: Epidermophyton, various: Trichophyton)
organisms.transmission: Direct contact (anthropophilic: human-to-human, zoophilic: animal-to-human, geophilic: soil-to-human), fomites
organisms.lifecycle: Colonizes keratinized tissue only (no deep invasion in immunocompetent hosts), digests keratin for nutrition
clinicalManifestations: Tinea corporis (body), capitis (scalp), pedis (athlete's foot), cruris (groin), unguium (nails, onychomycosis)
Annular, scaly, pruritic lesions with central clearing
organisms.diagnosis: KOH direct exam (septate branching hyphae), culture on Sabouraud agar, Wood's lamp (some Microsporum fluoresce)
organisms.treatment: Topical antifungals (terbinafine, azoles) for skin; oral terbinafine/itraconazole for nails/scalp
organisms.geographicDistribution: Worldwide

organisms.morphology: Septate hyphae with acute-angle (45°) branching, conidiophores with characteristic conidial heads on culture
organisms.transmission: Inhalation of airborne conidia (ubiquitous in environment, decaying matter)
organisms.lifecycle: Inhaled conidia germinate in lungs; disease severity depends on host immune status and pre-existing lung disease
clinicalManifestations: Invasive pulmonary aspergillosis (in neutropenic/immunosuppressed — angioinvasive, high mortality)
organisms.diagnosis: Galactomannan antigen (serum/BAL), culture, CT ('halo sign' early, 'air-crescent sign' later in invasive disease), histopathology (septate hyphae, acute branching)
organisms.treatment: Voriconazole (invasive disease, first line); surgery for aspergilloma; corticosteroids + antifungal for ABPA
organisms.geographicDistribution: Worldwide (ubiquitous environmental mold)

organisms.morphology: Mucorales: broad, ribbon-like, non-septate (pauciseptate) hyphae with right-angle branching. Fusarium: septate hyphae, banana-shaped macroconidia on culture
organisms.transmission: Inhalation of spores, direct inoculation (trauma/burns)
organisms.lifecycle: Rapid angioinvasive growth causing tissue infarction and necrosis; strongly associated with uncontrolled diabetes (DKA) and neutropenia
clinicalManifestations: Rhino-orbito-cerebral mucormycosis (classic in DKA): black eschar, facial pain, orbital involvement
Fusarium: disseminated disease with skin lesions + positive blood cultures (unusual for molds) in neutropenic patients, keratitis
organisms.diagnosis: Histopathology (broad non-septate hyphae for Mucorales), culture, blood cultures often positive for Fusarium (unlike other molds)
organisms.treatment: Aggressive surgical debridement + liposomal amphotericin B (Mucorales); voriconazole (Fusarium)
organisms.geographicDistribution: Worldwide, increased incidence in uncontrolled diabetics and immunosuppressed (notable surge post-COVID in India)

organisms.morphology: Mycetoma: grains/granules of fungal (eumycetoma) or bacterial (actinomycetoma) origin. Sporothrix: dimorphic — mold at room temp, cigar-shaped yeast at body temp
organisms.transmission: Traumatic inoculation through skin (thorns, splinters, soil contact) — 'rose gardener's disease' for sporotrichosis
organisms.lifecycle: Local implantation → chronic granulomatous inflammation; sporotrichosis can spread along lymphatics
clinicalManifestations: Mycetoma: triad of tumefaction, sinus tracts, and grain discharge, usually on foot ('Madura foot')
Sporotrichosis: nodular lymphangitis — ascending chain of nodules/ulcers along lymphatic drainage from inoculation site
organisms.diagnosis: Grain examination/culture (mycetoma), culture at two temperatures for dimorphism (Sporothrix), histopathology
organisms.treatment: Itraconazole (sporotrichosis, eumycetoma); surgery + antibiotics for actinomycetoma
organisms.geographicDistribution: Mycetoma: 'mycetoma belt' (tropical Africa, India, Latin America). Sporotrichosis: worldwide, especially gardeners/agricultural workers

names.en: Dimorphic fungi (Histoplasma, Blastomyces, Coccidioides, Paracoccidioides, Talaromyces)

organisms.morphology: Mold form (environmental, 25°C) transitions to yeast/spherule form (tissue, 37°C) — Histoplasma (intracellular yeast), Blastomyces (broad-based budding yeast), Coccidioides (spherules with endospores), Paracoccidioides ('pilot's wheel' yeast), Talaromyces (fission yeast)
organisms.transmission: Inhalation of spores from environment (soil, bird/bat droppings for Histoplasma, desert dust for Coccidioides)
organisms.lifecycle: Inhaled spores convert to tissue form at body temperature → primary pulmonary infection → may disseminate, especially if immunocompromised
clinicalManifestations: Histoplasmosis: pulmonary disease, disseminated disease in AIDS (endemic Ohio/Mississippi River valleys)
Blastomycosis: pulmonary/cutaneous verrucous lesions (Great Lakes/Southeastern US)
Talaromycosis: disseminated disease in HIV, characteristic umbilicated skin lesions (Southeast Asia)
organisms.diagnosis: Urine/serum antigen (Histoplasma), culture requiring temperature shift, histopathology, serology
organisms.treatment: Itraconazole (mild-moderate); amphotericin B (severe/disseminated/CNS)
organisms.geographicDistribution: Geographically restricted per species (see clinical manifestations)

organisms.morphology: Composite topic covering Cryptosporidium, Isospora/Cystoisospora, Cyclospora, Toxoplasma, Microsporidia, Pneumocystis, Cryptococcus in the context of HIV/AIDS
organisms.transmission: Varies by organism (see individual entries)
organisms.lifecycle: Key concept: organisms that are self-limited in immunocompetent hosts become severe/chronic/disseminated once CD4 count falls below critical thresholds
clinicalManifestations: CD4 <50: disseminated MAC, CMV retinitis (non-parasitic reference point)
organisms.diagnosis: CD4 count correlates with risk profile; guides prophylaxis and differential diagnosis
organisms.treatment: Organism-specific treatment + ART initiation/optimization + prophylaxis per CD4 threshold
organisms.geographicDistribution: Worldwide, burden concentrated in high HIV-prevalence regions (Sub-Saharan Africa)
